summary: Updates RFC 7519 with practical guidance for implementing and deploying JSON Web Tokens securely. JWTs are widely used signed or encrypted tokens carrying claims, in digital identity and other areas, and this best current practice document describes how to avoid known pitfalls.

eli5.summary: A JWT is like a signed pass. This gives rules for making and checking passes so thieves cannot fake them.

questions: what is the jwt alg none attack
subtitle: A checklist of known JSON Web Token pitfalls and the minimum rules that avoid them.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Tokens spread quickly, and several widely published attacks hit libraries and applications that were under-specified, incompletely implemented or used incorrectly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists nine known threats, then gives twelve best practices that mitigate them, such as fixing the allowed algorithms, validating every cryptographic operation and checking the issuer and audience.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 7519 and sets a floor, not a ceiling, for secure JWT use. It is a point-in-time statement, so readers should look for errata and updates.

facts.label: NIST curves with required key validation

today: RFC 8725 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 225) published in February 2020 that updates RFC 7519. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the document itself advises readers to check for errata and updates.

sections.title: Why a Best Practices Document
sections.content:
JSON Web Tokens (JWTs, defined in RFC 7519) are URL-safe, JSON-based security tokens that carry a set of claims. The claims can be signed, encrypted or both. JWTs are used in digital identity, for example in OpenID Connect ID Tokens and OAuth 2.0 access and refresh tokens, and in other areas.

The RFC says that since the JWT specification was published there have been several widely published attacks on implementations and deployments. It blames under-specified security mechanisms, incomplete implementations and incorrect use by applications.

The recommendations are intended as minimum rules for the vast majority of deployments. Other specifications can be stricter, and stronger options are always allowed. The audience is JWT library implementers, developers of code that uses those libraries, and authors of specifications that rely on JWTs. Because knowledge about attacks changes quickly, the RFC calls itself a point-in-time statement and tells readers to look for errata or updates.
sections.eli5: Lots of people started using the same kind of signed pass, and some bad guys found tricks to fool the guards. This is a list of the tricks and how to stop them.

sections.title: Known Threats and Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
Section 2 describes nine problems, each pointing to the best practices that fix it.

  • Weak signatures and insufficient validation. The alg header says how a token is signed. Attackers can change it to none, and some libraries then accept the token with no signature check. An RS256 token can also be changed to HS256, so a library checks an HMAC using the RSA public key as the shared secret.
  • Weak symmetric keys. A human-memorable password used as an HS256 key can be brute-forced offline once an attacker has a token.
  • Incorrect composition of encryption and signature. Some libraries decrypt a JWE to get a signed object but do not always validate the inner signature.
  • Plaintext leakage through ciphertext length. Encryption leaks length, and compressing first makes the length depend on content too.
  • Insecure elliptic curve encryption. Some libraries do not validate inputs to ECDH-ES, which can let an attacker recover the recipient's private key using invalid curve points.
  • Multiplicity of JSON encodings. Older JSON specifications allowed UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, which can cause a token to be misread and checks to be bypassed.
  • Substitution attacks. A token meant for one recipient is replayed at another. Cross-JWT confusion is a specific kind of this, where a token issued for one purpose is used for another.
  • Indirect attacks on the server. Claims used for database or LDAP lookups, or that contain URLs, can carry injection or server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks.
sections.eli5: The RFC first lists the ways bad guys have fooled the guards: scribbling out the signature rule, using a password anyone can guess, or sneaking a pass meant for one door into another.

sections.title: Choosing and Verifying Algorithms
sections.content:
Libraries MUST let the caller specify a supported set of algorithms and MUST NOT use any others. The library MUST check that the alg or enc header names the same algorithm that is actually used, and each key MUST be used with exactly one algorithm. This blocks the none and RS256-to-HS256 tricks.

Applications MUST only allow cryptographically current algorithms that meet their needs, and MUST be designed for cryptographic agility, because the acceptable set changes over time. The none algorithm can be acceptable when the JWT is already protected end to end by other means such as TLS. Libraries SHOULD NOT generate or consume none JWTs unless the caller explicitly asks.

Two algorithm-specific recommendations: avoid all RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption algorithms and prefer RSAES-OAEP, and implement ECDSA with the deterministic approach of RFC 6979, because predictable random values can expose the private key. That approach needs no new algorithm identifiers.
sections.eli5: The guard keeps a short list of signature methods they trust and ignores a pass that claims a different method. A pass that says no signature needed gets turned away unless the guard was told to expect that.

sections.title: Validating Operations, Inputs and Keys
sections.content:
All cryptographic operations in the JWT MUST be validated, and the whole JWT MUST be rejected if any fail. For a Nested JWT, both the outer and the inner operations MUST be validated using keys and algorithms supplied by the application.

Inputs must be checked too. For ECDH-ES, the ephemeral public key (epk) should be validated against the recipient's chosen curve. For the NIST curves P-256, P-384 and P-521, validation MUST follow Section 5.6.2.3.4 of NIST SP 800-56A Revision 3. If X25519 or X448 are used, the security considerations of RFC 8037 apply.

Keys need enough entropy. The key entropy advice in RFC 7515 and the password considerations in RFC 7518 MUST be followed. Human-memorizable passwords MUST NOT be used directly as the key for a keyed MAC such as HS256. Passwords should only be used for key encryption, and even then they remain open to brute force.
sections.eli5: The guard checks every lock and every seal, including the one inside a sealed envelope. And the secret code must be truly hard to guess, not your pet's name.

sections.title: Compression and Character Encoding
sections.content:
Compression of data SHOULD NOT be done before encryption, because compressed data often reveals information about the plaintext through its length.

JSON in Header Parameters and JWT Claims Sets MUST be encoded as UTF-8. RFC 7515, RFC 7516 and RFC 7519 already say this, and it matches the latest JSON specification, RFC 8259. Implementations and applications MUST NOT use or admit other Unicode encodings for these purposes. This removes the ambiguity that a malicious sender could use to slip past validation.
sections.eli5: Do not squish a secret note before locking it, because the size of the squished note gives hints. And everyone writes in the same alphabet so no one reads it differently.

sections.title: Issuer, Subject and Audience Checks
sections.content:
When a JWT has an iss (issuer) claim, the application MUST validate that the keys used in the token's cryptographic operations belong to that issuer, and MUST reject the JWT if they do not. How keys are tied to issuers is application-specific. In OpenID Connect the issuer is an https URL pointing to a metadata document whose jwks_uri leads to the issuer's JWK Set.

When a JWT has a sub (subject) claim, the application MUST validate that the subject is valid, alone or as an issuer-subject pair. If the issuer, subject or pair are invalid, the JWT MUST be rejected.

If one issuer can issue tokens for more than one relying party, the JWT MUST contain an aud (audience) claim. The relying party MUST validate it, and MUST reject the JWT if the audience is missing or not associated with the recipient.

Received claims must not be trusted blindly. The kid header should be validated or sanitized so it cannot cause SQL or LDAP injection. The jku and x5u headers can hold arbitrary URLs, so applications SHOULD protect against SSRF, for example by matching the URL to a whitelist and sending no cookies in the GET request.
sections.eli5: The guard checks who wrote the pass, who it names, and which door it is for. A pass for the library does not open the bank.

sections.title: Telling Kinds of JWTs Apart
sections.content:
Sometimes one kind of JWT can be confused with another. Explicit typing uses the typ Header Parameter to say what kind a token is, and validation rules then check it. It is RECOMMENDED to omit the application/ prefix from the typ value. For example, Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417) use the media type application/secevent+jwt, so their typ SHOULD be secevent+jwt. For a Nested JWT, the typ MUST be present in the inner JWT. Explicit typing may not separate a new kind from existing kinds whose rules ignore typ, but it is RECOMMENDED for new uses of JWTs.

If one issuer can issue more than one kind of JWT, the validation rules MUST be written to be mutually exclusive, rejecting tokens of the wrong kind. The RFC suggests several strategies: explicit typing, different required claims or values, different required Header Parameters or values, different keys, different aud values, or different issuers. The best mix is application-specific.
sections.eli5: If the same office hands out library passes and gym passes, each pass should be clearly labeled and each door should only accept its own kind.
